meta.title: Who really said "Democracy and socialism have nothing in common but one word: equality. But notice the difference: while democracy seeks equality in liberty, socialism seeks equality in restraint and servitude"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Tocqueville really said it, in an 1848 speech to France's Constituent Assembly. But the famous English wording is Hayek's 1944 translation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Democracy and socialism have nothing in common but one word: equality. But notice the difference: while democracy seeks equality in liberty, socialism seeks equality in restraint and servitude'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Tocqueville — from his 12 September 1848 speech against the 'right to work'. The English everyone quotes comes from Hayek's The Road to Serfdom.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1805–1859 · French political thinker & deputy in the 1848 Constituent Assembly
answer.sourceLine: Tocqueville said it from the floor of the French Constituent Assembly on 12 September 1848, arguing against an amendment that would have written a “right to work” into the constitution of the Second Republic; the French text is printed in his Œuvres complètes, vol. IX (1866). The English sentence everyone quotes is F. A. Hayek’s rendering of those lines in The Road to Serfdom (1944), which footnotes the speech directly.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Discours prononcé à l’Assemblée constituante le 12 septembre 1848 sur la question du droit au travail
Œuvres complètes d’Alexis de Tocqueville, vol. IX (Paris: Lévy, 1866), p. 546
English wording from F. A. Hayek, The Road to Serfdom (University of Chicago Press, 1944), chap. II

source.excerpt: La démocratie étend la sphère de l’indépendance individuelle, le socialisme la resserre. La démocratie donne toute sa valeur possible à chaque homme, le socialisme fait de chaque homme un agent, un instrument, un chiffre. La démocratie et le socialisme ne se tiennent que par un mot, l’égalité ; mais remarquez la différence : la démocratie veut l’égalité dans la liberté, et le socialisme veut l’égalité dans la gêne et dans la servitude.
trail: The French original is on the page: the scanned volume 9 of the 1866 Œuvres complètes ↗ carries ‘la démocratie veut l’égalité dans la liberté, et le socialisme veut l’égalité dans la gêne et dans la servitude’ inside the speech on the right to work.

The English wording traces to one book: chapter II of Hayek’s The Road to Serfdom (University of Chicago Press, 1944) ↗ quotes the passage verbatim and footnotes it to ‘Discours prononcé à l’assemblée constituante le 12 septembre 1848 sur la question du droit au travail,’ Œuvres complètes (1866), IX, 546.
Wikiquote ↗ lists it among his sourced 1840s quotations with the same citation and credits the translation to Hayek — it is not filed under Disputed or Misattributed.

Biography checks out against the setting: Tocqueville (1805–1859) ↗ was elected to the Constituent Assembly of 1848 and served on the commission drafting the Second Republic’s constitution, so he was in the chamber for exactly this debate.
source.excerptNote: The original French, as printed in the 1866 Œuvres complètes. The English sentence in circulation today is Hayek’s 1944 translation of exactly these lines.

source.rightsNote: Two different clocks run here. Tocqueville’s French — spoken in 1848, printed in the 1866 Œuvres complètes — is long in the public domain. The English wording quoted above is a different work: it first appeared in F. A. Hayek’s The Road to Serfdom (University of Chicago Press, 1944), so that translation is still under copyright in the United States. Quote the French freely; treat the familiar English as a copyrighted translation and keep excerpts short and attributed.

author.name: Alexis de Tocqueville
author.heading: Who was Alexis de Tocqueville?
author.metaLine: 1805–1859 · French political thinker, historian & deputy in the 1848 Constituent Assembly
author.bio: Alexis de Tocqueville (1805–1859) is best known for Democracy in America, which appeared in two volumes in 1835 and 1840 after his tour of the United States, and for The Old Regime and the Revolution (1856). He was not only an observer of politics but a participant in it: elected to France’s Constituent Assembly in 1848, he sat on the commission that drafted the Second Republic’s constitution. This quote comes from that working life — a speech in a live constitutional debate, not from a book.

misattribution.heading: What gets garbled
misattribution.intro: For once the famous name is the right one — Tocqueville really did say this. What travels loosely is where it comes from and whose English it is.

items.who: The English is F. A. Hayek’s, 1944
items.why: Tocqueville spoke French. The exact sentence quoted today — ‘nothing in common but one word: equality… equality in restraint and servitude’ — is the rendering Hayek printed in chapter II of The Road to Serfdom (1944) ↗, introduced with ‘he said in 1848’ and footnoted to the speech. Quoting it as Tocqueville’s own words is true of the thought, not of the phrasing.

items.who: An 1848 floor speech, not Democracy in America
items.why: Tocqueville’s famous book is not the source. The line belongs to his speech to the Constituent Assembly on the question of the right to work ↗, published posthumously in the Œuvres complètes of 1866.

The French reads that socialism makes of each man un agent, un instrument, un chiffre — an agent, an instrument, a number — per the 1866 printed page ↗. The English that circulates gives only ‘a mere agent, a mere number’, quietly losing ‘instrument’.

Some sites do carry the correct citation, but plenty do not: Goodreads ↗ presents the passage with no source line at all, tagged only ‘theroadtoserfdom’ — which points at the translator’s book rather than at Tocqueville’s speech.

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution holds up: the sentence is Tocqueville’s, delivered on 12 September 1848 and printed in the 1866 Œuvres complètes ↗. What you are reading in English, though, is Hayek.

context.heading: Why it was said
lead: The setting was a constitutional drafting fight, not a philosophy seminar. In 1848 Tocqueville was an elected member of France’s Constituent Assembly and sat on the commission writing the Second Republic’s constitution. On 12 September he rose to oppose an amendment that would have enshrined a droit au travail — a right to work — and the passage everyone quotes is the rhetorical hinge of that speech: his attempt to separate the democratic revolution he supported from the socialist one he did not.

The sentence reached English readers largely through one book. In The Road to Serfdom (1944), Hayek introduced it with the line that nobody saw more clearly than Tocqueville that democracy stood in irreconcilable conflict with socialism, then quoted the passage and footnoted the 1848 speech. That is the version that has circulated ever since.
context.detailsSummary: What Tocqueville actually said, in French
detailsBody: The French runs: « La démocratie et le socialisme ne se tiennent que par un mot, l’égalité ; mais remarquez la différence : la démocratie veut l’égalité dans la liberté, et le socialisme veut l’égalité dans la gêne et dans la servitude. » You can read it in context in the 1866 Œuvres complètes text on Wikisource ↗.

La gêne is the word doing the heavy lifting: it means constraint, hardship, straitened circumstances. “Restraint” is a defensible English choice, but it hardens a word that in French also carries the sense of being pinched or hard-up.
context.pull: The line is genuinely Tocqueville’s — but the memorable English is Hayek’s.

schema.quotationText: Democracy extends the sphere of individual freedom, socialism restricts it. Democracy attaches all possible value to each man; socialism makes each man a mere agent, a mere number. Democracy and socialism have nothing in common but one word: equality. But notice the difference: while democracy seeks equality in liberty, socialism seeks equality in restraint and servitude.
